cases.title: The Bahrain Grand Prix and the 2012-2014 Protest Crackdown
cases.place: Shakhura and other villages near Manama, and the Bahrain International Circuit at Sakhir, Bahrain
cases.point: Shakhura, the village north-west of Manama where the body of Salah Abbas Habib was found on a roof on 21 April 2012, about a kilometre from the previous day's protest. Coordinates from the US NGA GEOnet gazetteer entry for Shakhura.

lenders.name: Formula One group companies (United Kingdom)
lenders.role: Formula One World Championship Limited and Formula One Management Limited hold the commercial rights to the Formula One World Championship. Formula One World Championship told the UK National Contact Point that it is contractually obliged to propose the Bahrain Grand Prix for the race calendar, and that the race itself is organised with a Bahrain event promoter that is partly state-owned (UK NCP initial assessment, October 2014).

cases.conditions: No loan or lending conditions were found; the money here runs the other way, from a partly state-owned Bahraini promoter to the holders of the racing rights. Formula One World Championship told the UK NCP that it was contractually obliged to propose the Bahrain Grand Prix for the calendar. The contract is not published, and the company declined to give the NCP further information, saying the NCP could not enforce confidentiality (UK NCP initial assessment, October 2014).

companies.name: Formula One World Championship Limited
companies.role: Holder of the commercial rights to the championship; responded to the complaint for the group
companies.desc: A UK company that holds the commercial rights to the Formula One World Championship and proposes the races that make up the calendar. It replied to the UK NCP for itself and as agent and business manager for Formula One Management Limited, and described its role as promoter, separate from the FIA, the sport's governing body.

companies.name: Formula One Management Limited
companies.role: Co-holder of the commercial rights; second respondent accepted for examination
companies.desc: A UK company in the Formula One group that holds commercial rights to the championship alongside Formula One World Championship Limited, which acts as its agent and business manager.

companies.name: Delta 3 (UK) Limited
companies.role: Respondent; the NCP did not pursue the issues against it
companies.desc: A UK company in the Formula One group ownership chain. The UK NCP decided not to pursue the complaint against it because it is not an operational company and so has no role in addressing the issues raised.

companies.name: Beta D3 Limited
companies.role: Respondent; the NCP did not pursue the issues against it
companies.desc: A UK company in the Formula One group ownership chain, which the UK NCP also found was not an operational company.

cases.community: Salah Abbas Habib, 37, was shot dead by security forces after protests in Manama on the Grand Prix weekend in April 2012, and his family was not allowed to see his body for three days (Amnesty International). Human Rights Watch reports that he was killed in Shakhura and that a Bahraini government report said he “was arrested and assaulted, and then shot with [a] shotgun”. Al Jazeera reported that his body was found on a roof about a kilometre from the previous day's protest, with a respirator mask around his neck. The following year, on 13 April 2013, security forces were reported to have shot 18-year-old Sara Ismail in the head with a tear gas canister in Samaheej, and she needed medical attention (Human Rights Watch). Races were held in Bahrain in 2012, 2013 and 2014.
cases.suppression: Between 1 and 10 April 2013, in the run-up to that year's race, security forces raided homes in towns near the circuit and detained at least 20 people, among them well-known anti-government activists (Human Rights Watch). Nafeesa al-'Asfoor, 31, and Rayhana al-Mousawi, 38, were arrested in 2013 after trying to enter the circuit to protest against political imprisonments, and were charged with terrorism intent and explosives offences; both said they were tortured and made to sign confessions they later withdrew, and al-Mousawi was given a separate five-year sentence in September 2013 (Amnesty International). A policeman tried over the killing of Salah Abbas Habib was acquitted in November 2013 for lack of evidence, and Amnesty International recorded no other prosecution.
cases.killed_note: Salah Abbas Habib was shot dead by Bahraini security forces on the 2012 race weekend, not by the companies or by anyone acting for them, so no death is counted against this entry. Amnesty International gives the date of the shooting as 20 April 2012; Human Rights Watch places the killing during protests on 21 April 2012, the day Al Jazeera reported the body was found.
cases.outcome: The UK NCP received the complaint on 11 June 2014 and published its initial assessment on 22 October 2014. It accepted for examination the questions of due diligence, human rights policy and communication with people affected, in relation to Formula One World Championship Limited and Formula One Management Limited; it rejected the issues framed as broad obligations to avoid or address adverse impacts, and declined to pursue the complaint against Delta 3 (UK) Limited and Beta D3 Limited because they are not operational companies. Formula One World Championship denied the allegations, said it did not consider mediation appropriate or necessary, and questioned the complainants' mandate. Mediation nonetheless followed, on 28 January and 8 April 2015, and the parties signed a joint statement on 10 April 2015 in which the Formula One group reaffirmed its commitment to internationally recognised human rights and undertook to strengthen its human rights processes. ADHRB stopped pursuing the complaint, the NCP closed the case, and it made no finding on whether the companies had acted consistently with the Guidelines. Because the agreement did not provide for one, the NCP issued no follow-up statement, so there is no public check on whether the commitments were carried out.

cases.confidence_note: The killing of Salah Abbas Habib, the 2013 raids and detentions near the circuit, and the injury to Sara Ismail are recorded by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Al Jazeera, outside the complaint. Who carried them out is also outside dispute: Bahraini security forces, not the companies. What is disputed is the companies' link to them. Formula One World Championship denied the allegations and told the UK NCP that stakeholder views were mixed, with some human rights representatives supporting the event; the NCP accepted only the due diligence, policy and engagement questions for examination, and in the end made no finding on whether the companies had met the Guidelines. The date of the shooting also differs between sources: Amnesty International says 20 April 2012, Human Rights Watch says the protests of 21 April 2012.

cases.whole: The races went ahead: Bahrain held a Grand Prix in 2012, 2013 and 2014, after the 2011 race was cancelled. What the complaint produced was a document rather than a change on the ground. The Formula One group reaffirmed its commitment to internationally recognised human rights, pointed to a written policy it had published, and undertook to take further steps to strengthen its human rights processes; those are the company's own undertakings, recorded by the UK NCP in May 2015, and the NCP's statement does not say what the further steps are. The NCP made no finding on whether the companies had met the Guidelines, and because the parties' agreement did not provide for a follow-up statement, no public check on the undertakings was ever made.

drops.why: The torture and indefinite detention at Guantánamo are documented elsewhere, but they were carried out by the US military, and no source outside the complaint ties G4S's janitorial and base-support contract, held through a US subsidiary it then sold, to harm done to any named person.

Duplicate of the Itochu entry above and of the existing case batang-coal-jbic; the two complaints are one event against two owners of the same joint venture.
The Jalaur dam and the December 2020 Tumandok killings are already on the map as jalaur-dam-tumandok-killings, with Daewoo named as contractor, so this is an extend to that case, not a new one.

The harm described, a 2003 lease of about 17,000 acres of Yala Swamp by a US-owned rice operation with aerial spraying and blocked lake access, is already on the map as dominion-farms-yala-swamp; the US NCP anonymised the company, so this is an extend to that case rather than a new one.

No source outside the complaint could be found for any of the harms, neither the dismissal and 4.5-year imprisonment of the worker representative in Bukavu nor the alleged discharge into Lake Kivu; searches in English and French returned only the complaint and the Luxembourg NCP's jurisdictional assessment.

Test 2 fails: the Bawdwin mine had not operated since 2009, and the complaint and the Australian NCP's findings concern the absence of due diligence, disclosure and stakeholder engagement around a divestment, with the displacement and sexual violence named as risks that development of the mine might bring rather than as harm that happened.

The harms at these coal plants, found likely to have occurred by the IFC's Compliance Advisor Ombudsman, are already on the map as rcbc-coal-plants; Standard Chartered belongs there as a co-lender and this complaint as a cx entry, not as a second case on the same plants.
